newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma says politics behind unrest, situation calm.
newsitem.headline: Burma says politics behind unrest, situation calm.

text.p: Burma's military government on Tuesday said recent religious strife in the country was politically motivated by people aiming to destabilise the nation, but that the situation was now under control.
However, the government would not comment on the fate of some 100 monks who were apparently detained over the weekend in the capital after they vandalised Moslem property and held a demonstration.
Witnesses said they saw about 100 monks being taken away in trucks on Sunday following several different attacks on Moslem buildings and a street demonstration.

"On the surface it seems like a religious clash but it is actually very much politically motivated," the government said in a statement received in Bangkok, in reference to recent clashes between Buddhists and Moslems in various Burmese cities.

"The anti-government groups are very much desperate to create instability in the country wherever or whenever possible," said the statement, the first issued by the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) since the troubles began on March 15.
It said the government had imposed a curfew in parts of Mandalay, where the clashes began, and implemented "appropriate security measures" to improve the situation and prevent further trouble.
The unrest began in Burma's second city of Mandalay 10 days ago when monks went on a rampage, attacking several mosques and staging street protests.

The government said the trouble was started by rumours that a Buddhist girl was molested by a Moslem. But others sources said it was sparked by reports that an important Buddha image in Mandalay had been vandalised.
The government also said minor damage had been inflicted on some personal properties and mosques, but that there had been no injuries and the situation was under control.
Diplomats and residents said on Tuesday the recent tension between Buddhists and Moslems seemed to be easing, but said there was still a very strong military presence in the streets.
"Things are cooler now, the authorities have taken moves to defuse the situation," said one diplomat.
Security continued to be beefed up around key Buddhist and Moslem sites, especially in the capital, to ensure attacks would not resume, diplomats and residents said.
Armed troops and barricades were set up near Buddhist monasteries and in Moslem communities mainly at night in Rangoon as security was relaxed during the day, residents said.
Several mosques and other Moslem buildings in Rangoon were attacked by Buddhist monks over the past few days.

But the government said the real reason behind the unrest was political, an attempt to create problems for Burma in its effort to become a full member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) this year.
ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines and Vietnam. Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia have mostly Moslem populations.
An official of opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy said the pro-democracy group had nothing to do with the recent unrest.
"We are very interested in what is going on, but we only know what we hear as rumours around here," the official told Reuters. "Whenever anything happens they say it involves us."
